old_title: England v Sri Lanka: second men's one-day cricket international - live
new_title: Sri Lanka beat England by 16 runs: second men's one-day cricket international - as it happened
old_text:
1st over: Sri Lanka 1-0 (Nissanka 1, Kamindu Mendis 0) Headingley is usually a great place to bat, so Sri Lanka will probably want upwards of 300. Fifty overs is a long time*, which means Kamindu Mendis can take a bit of time to get his eye in. He plays out five consecutive dot balls during an accurate opening over from Archer.
There was something about Dan Lawrence's pained groan at Edgbaston in England's first innings of the third Test against Pakistan. For a split second it looked as if he might plunge his bat into the turf like some tormented Norse warrior. His stumps had already been flattened by his own hand, an attempt to run the ball down past point off Mohammad Imran had ended in him hacking an innocuous delivery emphatically on to them.
The stump microphone amplified Lawrence's anguished reaction, the noise emanating from his mouth oscillating somewhere between the visceral howl of treading on an upturned plug and the disappointed yelp of missing the last train home. He had been bowled for 65 and another chance of a first Test century had gone begging.
Test batters will tell you how they didn't feel they "belonged" until they had made a century. That the longer they had to wait to cross the Rubicon of three figures the more it weighed them down. Lawrence has played 17 Tests for England since his first call-up in 2021. It has been a career of fits and starts through no fault of his own; in the past five years he has batted at Nos 7, 6, 5, 4 and 3 as well as a doomed stint as a makeshift opener. It's those starts that will eat away at him, though.
South Africa's Matthew Breetzke has continued the spectacular start to his ODI career. He's currently 84 not out against Australia in Durban; you can follow that game with Martin Pegan and Geoff Lemon.
To reach for the career stats on Cricinfo is no way to go about it. This is a full-on YouTube job: boil the kettle, load up those spells at Headingley, St Lucia and the rest, and take in the whippy, absurd, mesmerising sight of perhaps the fastest English bowler there has ever been. That's probably the best way to remember Mark Wood's career.
Tuesday's announcement of his international retirement was coming from the moment Wood hobbled out of the Ashes last December, the series opener his only appearance. That always felt like the last act, one he rushed back for after surgery on his left knee earlier that year, and the game moves on fast. England's seam stocks look healthy across formats, with Jofra Archer there to ramp it up when required. It's a sore point that Archer and Wood played just two Tests together: one without supporters during the 2020 Covid-bubble summer, the other Wood's farewell at Perth.
The 36-year-old leaves with 119 Test wickets at 30.8 and 80 one-day international wickets at 40.8, figures that need dissecting. He sparkled when it mattered in 50-over cricket, taking 18 wickets in the 2019 World Cup triumph, and there is a clear before-and-after with the red ball. Having made his debut in 2015, it took nearly four years for it all to click together, only after Wood lengthened his run-up and was told by Trevor Bayliss that he wanted to see a bit more "mongrel" from his quick.
Wood responded by clocking 95mph on the way to his first Test five-wicket haul, against West Indies in February 2019 at the age of 29, setting up his own Benjamin Button tale. From that Test in St Lucia, his 13th, until his last, he averaged 27, all while hurling the ball with a lithe frame at obscene, unhealthy speeds.
Harry Brook had called on his England players to continue the "high-octane" cricket witnessed during their clean sweep in the Twenty20s but this latest victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international was more of a slow-burn affair.
Gone was the neck-arching carnage of the previous week and in its place, on a tired end-of-season surface, England were bowled out for 265 in 48.1 overs. Brook top-scored with 67 under a warm September sun, before his bowlers rolled the tourists for 176 to take a 1-0 lead into Thursday's second match at Headingley.
Familiarity with conditions doubtless played its part and Sri Lanka, on the wrong side of the toss, never truly felt in the hunt. For Brook it was an 11th victory as England's ODI captain, nudging him into credit after 10 defeats and continuing what has been a quiet resurgence in the format this year.
It's been a while*, you know. Since England won three ODI series in a row; it's been a while. The last time it happened was in 2023, just before the World Cup, when everything was going to be alright on the night.
That grisly title defence was the start of a desperate few years in ODI cricket, but there are signs that Brendon McCullum is giving England the kiss of life in a third format. If they beat Sri Lanka at Headingley today - and it'll be an eye-widener if they don't - England will complete a third series victory of 2026.
At this stage they are no more than dangerous outsiders for next year's World Cup, but even that would have been unimaginable during the annus horribilis of 2025. England lost 11 out of 15 ODIs and their captain was almost ironed out by a bouncer the night before a game. Off and especially on the field, it feels like a long time ago.
* If these four words made your brain jump straight to a Linoleum song, you win an ephemeral trip back to 1997.
new_text:
Kusal Mendis is the player of the match for his century but he also deserves credit for a big call with the ball: continuing with Sachindu Colombage after Jos Buttler tucked into him, leading to the wicket of Joe Root.
After four comprehensive defeats, Sri Lanka are finally up and running on this tour. The turning point has to be Jos Buttler's injury, tweaking his left hamstring when the game was heading England's way. In the end, the matchwinners are Kusal Mendis with his 121 and Dunith Wellalage with his three wickets.
49.3: WHAT A STOP! Archer smashes the ball down the ground for what seems a certain six, but Kamindu Mendis leaps to his left to keep it in. It's, well, a dropped catch ... but let's not be silly.
49th over: England 303-8 (Buttler 69, Archer 0) Archer can't get Malinga away and England need 19 from the last over, with Buttler - in serious pain - on strike.
WICKET! Jacks c Liyanage b Malinga 52 (England 303-8)
Buttler tries a scoop but doesn't get any bat on it. He then awkwardly swishes to long-off and hobbles again for one. Malinga nails his yorker to Jacks, who is swinging for the hills now. And he goes! The ball flies high into the sky and Janith Liyanage runs in from long-on to collect. Jacks can't finish the job tonight.
48th over: England 302-7 (Buttler 68, Jacks 52) Buttler returns with a dodgy left hamstring and is clearly in pain as he swings away for one. And Jacks middles the last ball of the over for a straight six! What a game! England need 20 from 12 balls.
WICKET! Overton c Asalanka b Fernando 2 (England 295-7)
Overton crunches Fernando to long-off for one before Jacks swings to the square-leg rope for four! That's the first boundary in years! The yorker follows before a full toss ... Overton doesn't middle it and Asalanka takes a brilliant grab running back to mid-off! There's a check to see if it's a waist-high no-ball but I think it'll be OK ... and it is.
WICKET! Atkinson c Rathnayake b Malinga 16 (England 288-6)
Malinga sends in a fierce yorker, living up to his name. An off-cutter follows and Jacks can't connect properly. And then another terrific, reverse-swinging yorker that Jacks plays back to the bowler.
Oh, that feels harsh from the umps, calling a wide on a slower ball. That looked OK to me. And then, finally, a wicket! Atkinson pulls straight to deep midwicket and Malinga fully deserves it. Sri Lanka are well in control here.
46th over: England 285-5 (Atkinson 15, Jacks 40) Atkinson dives to make his ground at the non-striker's end and takes a blow to the helmet from the throw directed at the stumps. Ow. Jacks flicks down the leg-side but Kusal Mendis makes a vital stop to deny a boundary. Fernando continues to search for the toe-thumping yorker before surprising Atkinson with a bouncer. This is strong death bowling, and I reckon this is Sri Lanka's game now. England need 37 from 24 balls.
45th over: England 280-5 (Atkinson 12, Jacks 38) Wellalage rips the ball past the outside edge and narrowly misses off-stump. The dots are really piling up now for England, with Atkinson getting a big forward-defence out. The left-arm spinner concedes just one as Atkinson keeps the strike and he finishes with figures of three for 49. England need 42 from 30 balls.
44th over: England 279-5 (Atkinson 11, Jacks 38) Asitha Fernando finds Atkinson's front pad and roars in appeal ... but that looks to be sliding down the leg-side. But he's out the next ball! It's a tailing yorker, one of Fernando's specialities, and Atkinson's going to review after being hit on the toes ... that's sliding down leg I reckon. Yep, just missing.The barest of margins. Nonetheless, it is another dot ball, that required rate climbing. A wide helps England and they need 43 from 36 balls.
42nd over: England 269-5 (Atkinson 5, Jacks 35) Madushanka is keeping it very tight from around the wicket, with Atkinson taking a single after a couple of dots. The seamer opts for a slower-ball bouncer to Jacks, who remains calm. The equation still favours England as these two keep churning out ones.
41st over: England 265-5 (Atkinson 3, Jacks 33) Colombage is back, that required rate above six now. Rathnayake has been great at short extra cover and makes another diving stop there. Jacks and Atkinson have to settle for singles. England need 57 from 54 balls.
WICKET! Ahmed c Kusal Mendis b Madushanka 0 (England 259-5)
Jacks very nearly punches into extra cover's hands off Madushanka, who gets Ahmed! The seamer goes short and the batter gets a bit of glove down the leg-side, failing with his pull shot.
39th over: England 256-4 (Ahmed 0, Jacks 27) A good stop at short extra cover from Rathnayake keeps Jacks on strike as Wellalage tries to squeeze out a few dots. Rehan Ahmed gets the forward defence out and it's a good over for Sri Lanka. England need 66 from 66 balls.
